place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 山门 · 石壁
place.en: Chending Temple · The gate · the stone wall

setup.zh: 二试，脑子：一面石壁，刻着九个空格，一堆刻了数的石块。「横竖斜，加起来都要一样。」
setup.en: Second trial, wits: a stone wall carved with nine empty squares, a heap of numbered stones. "Across, down, corner to corner — they all add up the same."

recap.zh: 二试，洛书九宫：你想起娘教的口诀，「五居中央」。
recap.en: Second trial, the Luo Shu square: you remembered Mother's rhyme — "five in the middle."

en: A stone wall, nine empty squares.
"Across, down, corner to corner — all the same."

story.zh:
一试下来，站在石阶顶上的，不过四五百人。送考的家里人，这时候也许从山侧一条小路绕上来，在山门外头等着。二试考脑子，在山门里头的一片石坪上。石坪上立着几十面石壁，每面石壁上刻着九个空格，横三竖三，像一张棋盘；石壁底下堆着九块石头，每块刻一个数，从一到九。一个管二试的老执事，背着手在石壁前走来走去，道：「横着加，竖着加，斜着加，都要一样。一炷香。」

有人把石头摆成了一朵花，有人摞成了一座塔，有人两块两块地换来换去，换了半炷香，越换越乱，把自己换哭了。还有一个孩子，盯着那九块石头看了很久很久，然后把它们一块一块，全都塞进了嘴里。老执事走过去，叹了口气，在那孩子背上一拍，「噗噗噗」，九块石头吐了一地。老执事对旁边的执事道：「每三年都有一个。」旁边那执事道：「今年这个塞得多，上一回那个只塞了五块。」老执事点点头，道：「一届比一届饿。」

石坪边上，隔开山门里外的，是一道矮墙。墙头上探着两颗脑袋，一颗是马家的家丁，一颗是葛六。葛六伸出指头来比划：先四根，再九根，再两根，一排一排地比，比得又快又稳，像镖局里对暗号。马小宝蹲在石壁底下，一面嚼桂花糕，一面照着比划摆石头。香才烧下去一小截，他已经拍拍手站了起来。横着加，十五；竖着加，十五；斜着加，还是十五。他摆完了，特地踱到小满跟前，伸着脖子看了一眼，道：「哟，沈小满，还没摆好？你娘没教你？」

他娘是教过的：「戴九履一，左三右七，二四为肩，六八为足，五居中央。」小满照着摆：五搁在正当中，头顶九，脚下一，左手三，右手七。摆到两个肩膀，一加，左边那一竖要凑十五，得有一块十。九块石头里，没有十。铜炉里那炷香，已经烧过了一半，马小宝在旁边嚼桂花糕，嚼得「吧唧吧唧」响。

墙头上，葛六的手指头还在比划，比给马小宝看的，小满也看得见：四，九，二。照着摆，一炷香都用不了。小满盯着那几根指头看了一会儿，把眼睛挪开了。马家的银子买来的东西，对，是马家的；错了，是一起死。他没有五两银子，也不想欠马家一个格子。可那几根手指头，倒叫他看出了一样东西：葛六冲着马小宝比划，站在墙那头，他的左手，是马小宝的右手。
story.en:
After the first trial, those standing at the top of the stair were no more than four or five hundred. The families who'd brought them were allowed up now by a path round the side of the mountain, to wait outside the gate. The second trial tested the head, on a stone terrace inside the gate. Dozens of stone walls stood on it, each carved with nine empty squares, three across and three down, like a game board; under each lay nine stones, each carved with a number from one to nine. The old steward in charge of the second trial paced before the walls, hands behind his back. "Add across, add down, add corner to corner — all the same. One stick of incense."

Some arranged the stones into a flower, some stacked them into a pagoda, some swapped them two by two back and forth for half a stick of incense, the more they swapped the worse it got, till they swapped themselves into tears. One boy stared at the nine stones a long, long time, and then put them one by one into his mouth, all nine. The old steward went over, sighed, and slapped him on the back — *pu, pu, pu* — nine stones spat out on the ground. The old steward said to the steward beside him: "Every three years there's one." The other said: "This year's stuffed in more. Last time's only managed five." The old steward nodded. "Hungrier every intake."

At the edge of the terrace a low wall divided inside the gate from out. Over the top of it peeked two heads: one a Ma servant, the other Ge Liu. Ge Liu was signing with his fingers: four, then nine, then two, row by row, fast and steady, like passwords at the escort bureau. Ma Xiaobao squatted at the foot of his wall, chewing osmanthus cake, setting stones by the signs. The incense had burned down only a little when he dusted off his hands and stood. Across, fifteen; down, fifteen; corner to corner, fifteen too. Finished, he strolled over to Xiaoman on purpose and craned his neck. "Well, Shen Xiaoman, not done yet? Didn't your mum teach you?"

His mother had: "Wear nine, tread one; three on the left, seven on the right; two and four for shoulders, six and eight for feet; five in the middle." Xiaoman set the stones by it: five in the middle, nine on the head, one under foot, three at the left hand, seven at the right. At the shoulders he added: to make fifteen down the left there would have to be a ten. Among nine stones there was no ten. The incense in the burner had burned past half; beside him Ma Xiaobao chomped his cake with loud smacks.

On the wall Ge Liu's fingers were still signing — signing for Ma Xiaobao, but Xiaoman could see them too: four, nine, two. Copy them, and it wouldn't take a stick of incense. Xiaoman watched those fingers a moment, and looked away. What Ma silver bought, if it was right, was the Mas'; if it was wrong, you went down together. He had no five taels, and didn't want to owe the Mas a single square. But the fingers did show him one thing: Ge Liu was signing toward Ma Xiaobao, from the far side of the wall — his left hand was Ma Xiaobao's right.

exits.means: hands in the solved square, or asks to go on to the third trial

refuse.zh: 九宫还没填满。瞿老不看半张卷子。
refuse.en: The square is not filled yet. Elder Qu does not look at half an answer.

story.zh:
小满闭上眼睛。是那一夜的炕桌，娘也是坐在他对面，一颗一颗挪栗子。娘嘴里的「左三」，是娘的左手；娘的左手，是他的右手。他记的肩膀，是自己眼里的；记的左右，是娘嘴里的——两样搁在一面墙上，自然凑不出十五。他把两个肩膀对调了一调：横着加，十五；竖着加，十五；斜着加，十五。炉里的香，还剩一小截。

老执事先踱到马小宝那面石壁前，看了一会儿，点点头，问道：「五为什么在中间？」马小宝一愣，眼睛往墙头上溜。墙头上，葛六急得伸出五根手指头，又拍了拍自己的肚子——意思是「五，正当中」。马小宝看明白了，大声道：「因为肚子在中间！」

石坪上登时笑成了一片。老执事顺着马小宝的眼睛往墙头上一看，看见了葛六，眉毛一挑：「葛六？」墙头上那颗脑袋「嗖」地缩了回去。老执事道：「二十年前，你那个『五』，也是背的。」他在马小宝的考牌上画了一笔——画的不是一道，是一个圈。马小宝的脸白了。

老执事又踱到小满跟前，问的还是那一句：「五为什么在中间？」小满道：「一配九，二配八，三配七，四配六，一对都是十，隔着中间那块，两头相望。九块石头，配剩下的，就是五。」老执事半天没说话，末了道：「谁教你的？」小满道：「口诀是我娘教的。为什么，是我方才算的。」

老执事「嗯」了一声，在他考牌上画了一道，却没有走，在石壁跟前一块石头上坐了下来，捶着腰道：「后人说，禹治水的时候得了这九个数，照着这九个格子，把天下分成了九州，又收了九州的铜，铸了九口鼎，一州一口。」说到这里，他顿了一顿，朝身后那座山看了一眼，声音低了些，「——这都是老辈子的话了。你娘教得好。你算得也好。」

小满把「九口鼎」三个字在嘴里嚼了一遍。九口大锅，一州一口，那得煮多少饭。他觉得胸口那块木牌好像动了一下，伸手去摸，却是凉的。

他转过身，石坪那一头，另一面石壁前，早有人摆好了——红鼻头，两根小辫子，蹲在石壁底下，拿炭条在一个蓝布面的小本子上低头记着什么。是阿禾。小满喊了一声，往那边挤了两步，人群一涌，再抬头看时，那石壁底下已经空了，只地上留着一截用秃了的炭条头。她是在躲他。
story.en:
Xiaoman shut his eyes. That night at the kang table, his mother sitting across from him too, moving the chestnuts one by one. The "three on the left" in her mouth was her left hand; her left hand was his right. The shoulders he'd remembered were as his own eyes saw them; the left and right he'd remembered were as her mouth said them — put both on one wall and of course they wouldn't make fifteen. He swapped the two shoulders: across, fifteen; down, fifteen; corner to corner, fifteen. A little stub of incense was left.

The old steward went first to Ma Xiaobao's wall, looked a while, nodded, and asked: "Why is five in the middle?" Ma Xiaobao froze, his eyes sliding to the top of the wall. On the wall, Ge Liu, frantic, held up five fingers and patted his own belly — meaning: "five, right in the middle". Ma Xiaobao got it and said loudly: "Because the belly's in the middle!"

The whole terrace burst out laughing. The old steward followed Ma Xiaobao's eyes up to the wall, saw Ge Liu, and raised an eyebrow. "Ge Liu?" The head on the wall shot down out of sight. The old steward said: "Twenty years ago, that 'five' of yours was learned by rote too." He drew a mark on Ma Xiaobao's tag — not a stroke: a circle. Ma Xiaobao's face went white.

The old steward strolled over to Xiaoman and asked the same: "Why is five in the middle?" Xiaoman said: "One with nine, two with eight, three with seven, four with six — every pair's ten, facing each other across the middle. Pair off nine stones, and what's left over is five." The old steward said nothing for a long while; at last: "Who taught you?" Xiaoman said: "The rhyme my mother taught me. The why, I just reckoned."

The old steward grunted, drew a stroke on his tag, but didn't leave; he sat down on a stone by the wall, thumped his back, and said: "Later people said Yu got these nine numbers while taming the flood, and by these nine squares divided the world into nine provinces, and gathered the bronze of the nine provinces and cast nine *ding*, one for each province." Here he paused, glanced at the mountain behind him, and lowered his voice. "— All old people's talk. Your mother taught you well. And you reckoned well."

Xiaoman chewed the words "nine *ding*" over once. Nine big pots, one a province — that would cook a lot of rice. He felt the token on his chest seem to stir; he reached for it, and it was cool.

He turned round. At the far end of the terrace, before another wall, someone had long since finished — red nose, two little braids, squatting at the foot of the wall, writing something with charcoal in a blue-cloth notebook. It was Ahe. Xiaoman called out and pushed two steps that way; the crowd surged, and when he looked up again the foot of the wall was empty, only a worn-down stub of charcoal left on the ground. She was avoiding him.
